## WENO3 and WENO5 (`type: weno3`, `weno5`) {#sec-ch04-weno}

<!-- PROVENANCE
pin: snapy@e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0 (chengcli/snapy)
sources: OUTLINE.md 4.6

### Summary

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
- A convex combination of candidate polynomials, weighted away from the rough ones by Jiang-Shu indicators.
- Switches: `type: weno3`, `type: weno5`. Only density and tracers use them; velocity and pressure take the
  matching linear polynomial (@sec-ch04-framework).
- Where the field is smooth the nonlinear weights approach the linear ones and the scheme becomes `cp3` or `cp5`.
- At a critical point WENO3 falls to second order. WENO5 does not, on the profile measured here.
- The smoothness floor is a fixed $10^{-6}$, not scaled to the magnitude of the data.
:::

WENO is the scheme that makes a high order survive a discontinuity. Instead of one wide stencil it builds
several narrow candidates, measures how rough each one looks, and takes a weighted average that all but
discards any candidate straddling a jump. Away from a jump the weights settle to fixed values chosen so that
the combination reproduces the wide centred polynomial.

### Derivation

Both forms share the same structure: candidates $p_k$, smoothness indicators $\beta_k$, linear weights $d_k$,
and nonlinear weights

$$
\alpha_k = \frac{d_k}{(\beta_k + \varepsilon)^2},\qquad
\phi_{\text{face}} = \frac{\sum_k \alpha_k p_k}{\sum_k \alpha_k},\qquad \varepsilon = 10^{-6}.
$$ {#eq-ch04-weno-weights}

The claim that makes the scheme high order is that the *linear* weights rebuild the wide polynomial exactly.
`[C2]` and `[C3]` check that symbolically, not numerically, and both differences are identically zero: with
$d = (\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$ the two WENO3 candidates rebuild `cp3`, and with $d = (\tfrac3{10}, \tfrac6{10},
\tfrac1{10})$ the three WENO5 candidates rebuild `cp5`. So wherever the indicators are equal, these schemes
*are* the centred polynomials of @sec-ch04-cp.

What the smoothness indicators then do is break that equality near a jump. They are the Jiang-Shu forms, sums
of squared undivided differences, at `beta0` ([`interp_simple.hpp:99-100`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L99-L100)) and
[`interp_simple.hpp:141-146`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L141-L146).

The order a WENO scheme attains in practice is not the order of its linear weights, and the chapter measures
both regimes rather than quoting the design figure. `[C4]` finds, over $n_1 = 16 \to 64$ on a monotone profile
with no critical point, fitted orders of 2.98 for WENO3 and 5.00 for WENO5: the design orders. Through two
critical points, over $n_1 = 32 \to 256$, WENO3 falls to a fitted 2.09 while the linear `cp3` on the same
profile keeps 2.99. WENO5 keeps 5.62 there.

The WENO3 result is the expected behaviour of the Jiang-Shu weights, not a defect: at a critical point the
indicators of the two candidates become equal at leading order and the nonlinear weights fail to approach the
linear ones fast enough to preserve third order. It is nonetheless a property a user should know about, because
a smooth field full of extrema, which is what a resolved wave field is, is reconstructed at second order by a
scheme named for its third.

### Numerical method

The two interpolants are `interp_weno3` ([`interp_simple.hpp:94-106`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L94-L106)) and
`interp_weno5` ([`interp_simple.hpp:134-153`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L134-L153)), written out in full with the candidates, the indicators and the
weights in the order of @eq-ch04-weno-weights. The measured orders are drawn in @fig-ch04-cp-order.

The floor $\varepsilon$ is the literal `1e-6` inside both bodies. It is not scaled by the magnitude of the
data, so for a field whose squared differences are far below $10^{-6}$ the floor dominates every indicator, all
$\alpha_k$ collapse to the $d_k$, and the scheme silently becomes its linear partner. For a field far above it
the floor is irrelevant. Neither regime is wrong, but the crossover depends on the units the deck is written
in, and nothing warns at it.

Only `interp1` is a WENO interpolant. Under `weno5` the density and tracer rows are reconstructed by
`interp_weno5` ([`interp_simple.hpp:134-153`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interp_simple.hpp#L134-L153)) while velocity and pressure take `cp5`, selected at
[`interpolation.cpp:29-36`](https://github.com/chengcli/snapy/blob/e894700ff7aee30b52882e5202b16461413780b0/src/recon/interpolation.cpp#L29-L36). A deck that chooses `weno5` to survive a shock therefore gets an
unlimited fifth-order linear reconstruction of its velocity and pressure through that same shock.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- WENO3 is second order at a critical point, measured at 2.09 here. If third order through smooth extrema is
  wanted, this interpolant does not provide it.
- The smoothness floor is an absolute $10^{-6}$. Whether it dominates the indicators depends on the units of
  the deck, and no warning is printed either way.
:::

1. **Only half the state is limited.** Velocity and pressure bypass WENO entirely. Whether that is the right
   split is a design question no source in the repository answers.
2. **Uniform-mesh weights.** As for the linear polynomials, the candidates and indicators assume equal cell
   widths.
3. **WENO5 through critical points.** The fitted 5.62 is above the design order and was measured on one
   profile over one ladder; it should be read as "did not degrade here", not as a general order claim.
